reason: Spelling variant of 'nerveless' (R0460), which is already accepted with the same target. The earlier review mapped veinless to vascular bundle absent (C349) and nerve to vascular bundle (C153, C273). The rule follows that.
PATO:0000947 elliptic has 'ellipsoid' as an exact synonym, so it covers the 3-D form. An olive is an ellipsoid solid. Same reading as 'broadly ellipsoid' (R0039) and 'long-ellipsoid' (R1443).
Two-jointed fruits (Cakile, Rapistrum) are jointed (FLOPO:0991154, 'one or more joints'). The count of two belongs in the count pattern, not in a new class.
In the floras it is used for five-angled outlines in cross-section (pedicels, 'in T.S.'). A cross-section is 2-D, so PATO:0040016 pentagonal (five angles and five sides) fits.
A child class of pinnatisect for 'twice pinnatisect' already exists (segments cut to their midribs again), so the double division is kept.
Same reading as 'broadly rhombic' (R0701) and 'short-rhomboid' (R1952). 'Short' only gives the length-to-width ratio, which PATO does not split.

Foliose pseudoparaphyllia are leaf-like rather than filamentous. Same mapping as 'narrowly foliose' (R1184). 'Broadly' is a width or degree word and is dropped. It is correctly not FLOPO leafy (bearing leaves).

Bryologists use 'lax' for cells that are large and thin-walled, but the thinness belongs to the cell wall, not the cell, and 'lax' does not state a thickness. This needs the part-of-the-bearer pattern (cell wall decreased thickness), not a word rule.

For a moss annulus, 'not separating' means it stays on the capsule mouth, which is persistent (PATO:0001732, as for 'persisting', R0385). For mericarps or valves it means not splitting or indehiscent, so the rule must be limited to the annulus.
The strength belongs to the stem. A word rule leaves robust on the whole plant. The right annotation is stem (PO:0009047) robust, which needs the part-of-the-bearer pattern.
The thickness belongs to the lateral walls of cells, not to the part named. Increased thickness on the bearer would be wrong. This needs the cell-wall part pattern.
The earlier review maps arcuate to PATO:0000406 curved (C185), so the negation is the matching rule. Floras use 'not arcuate' to contrast with straight. Same treatment as 'uncurved' (R1683).

Corolla spur (PO:0025512) is right for corolla and flower, as for 'ecalcarate' (R1392). Petal or lip spurs need petal spur (PO:0025511, as in 'spurless'). Leaf-base, sepal and anther spurs have no PO class.
Piliform means hair-like, and the earlier review mapped 'hair-like' to PATO:0104351 filiform (C317). Filiform's definition (long, very slender, round in section) covers hair-fine parts.

In the source rows the filaments or stipules are fused to each other up to the apex, which is connate (like parts). With other parts, 'fused to apex' of a different organ would be adnate (FLOPO:0991129).
'Repliable' is a mistranslation of French 'replié' (folded back on itself), not 'able to be folded'. So PATO:0001910 folded is right, as for 'complicate' (R0716).
'À points translucides' is pellucid-dotted, which is already a synonym of FLOPO:0991174 gland-dotted. In floras, translucent dots in the tissue are oil glands.
A positive class now exists for a set of homologous structures occurring in a single form. That is exactly homomorphous, and better than a negation of dimorphic.
Hyacinth scent is a heavy, sweet floral scent, covered by FLOPO:0991016 sweet-scented. The policy is not to create a scent class for each species compared to. The source words keep 'hyacinth'.
'Tight bunches of culms' is caespitose. 'Bunchy' fruits or flowers mean clustered, which is not a growth-habit tuft. The constraint matches the bearers of FLOPO:0991007.
Bland fruit has little or no flavour, the same as 'insipid' (R1381) and 'tasteless' (R0344). Those are unconstrained, and only tasted parts get taste words.
Glassy spines, bristles, hairs and fruits are translucent, as with pellucid (C237). On leaf or stem surfaces 'glassy' often means glossy, so the rule should not apply there.
There is no hirtellous class. The head value puberulous carries the compound, as caudate-acuminate maps to caudate (R0007). The stiffness stays in the source words.
The tips end in a small, stiff, spine-like bristle, which spine-tipped (FLOPO:0991210) states. An awn present can be added from the separate 'aristate' rule.
An abrupt short stiff point is FLOPO:0991054 mucronate, as for 'pungent-apiculate' (R1361). The callose tip could be added as FLOPO:0991215 callose, but it does not make this rule wrong.
Both shapes hold (a tail ending in a stiff point), not a range. Caudate is the more specific, as decided for 'caudate-acuminate' (R0007).
A much-branched inflorescence with cymes as its last branches resembles a panicle. Thyrse-like (FLOPO:0991199) would assume an indeterminate main axis, which the word does not state.
Fat stems, branches and mid-lobes are thick (PATO:0000591, synonym stout). For seeds or fruits 'fat' means plump or broad, which is not thickness.
'Hardly expanded' means scarcely or not widened. 'Not expanded' already maps to 'not dilated' (R0300), and the degree word stays as a cue in the record.

PATO:0001891 ovate carries 'ovoid' as a synonym and is used for the 3-D egg shape. 'Long-' is a proportion word and is dropped, as for 'long-ellipsoid' (R1443). Recheck when pato#627 splits ovate from ovoid.
